title: Claude Code Dynamic Workflows
content:
## Overview

**Dynamic workflows** (introduced May 2026, generally available with Opus 4.8) are Claude Code's answer to a problem the manager/subagent pattern hits at scale: past 3-5 parallel subagents, the coordinator's context window fills up with intermediate results and it starts losing track of the overall task. Instead of Claude dispatching subagents turn by turn and reading every result back into its own context, Claude writes a **JavaScript orchestration script** that a separate runtime executes — fanning work out across 10s to 100s of subagents in the background while the main session stays responsive.

---

## How It Differs From Regular Subagents

| | Manager/worker subagents | Dynamic workflows |
|---|---|---|
| Orchestration logic | Lives in Claude's context, turn by turn | Lives in a script, executed by a runtime |
| Practical fan-out limit | ~3-5 concurrent tasks before context saturates | 10s-100s of concurrent agents |
| Control flow | Implicit, re-decided each turn | Explicit: loops, conditionals, pipelines |
| Result handling | Every result re-enters Claude's context | Only what the script returns re-enters context |

The architectural shift is that Claude becomes **the planner, not the dispatcher** — it authors the script once, and the runtime (not Claude) drives execution, checks results, and re-runs failed stages.

---

## Script Primitives

A workflow script is plain JavaScript (no TypeScript syntax) built around a small set of hooks:

- **`agent(prompt, opts)`** — spawns one subagent and returns its result; `opts.schema` forces a structured JSON return instead of free text
- **`pipeline(items, ...stages)`** — runs each item through a chain of stages with **no barrier between stages**, so item A can reach stage 3 while item B is still on stage 1. This is the default shape for multi-stage work because wall-clock time tracks the slowest single chain, not the sum of per-stage worst cases
- **`parallel(thunks)`** — runs tasks concurrently but **is a barrier**: it waits for every thunk before returning. Reserved for cases that genuinely need all prior results at once (deduplication before an expensive stage, early-exit on a zero count)
- **`phase(title)` / `log(message)`** — grouping and progress-reporting for the user-facing view

Concurrency within a single workflow is capped (roughly the number of CPU cores minus a couple, up to a fixed ceiling), and a hard cap of about 1,000 total agent calls per workflow acts as a runaway-loop backstop.

---

## Quality Patterns

Because a script — not Claude's judgment turn-by-turn — controls the fan-out, workflows are the natural place to build in adversarial rigor:

- **Adversarial verify:** spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each told to try to refute it; a finding survives only if a majority fail to refute it
- **Loop-until-dry:** keep spawning "finder" agents (for bugs, edge cases, etc.) until several consecutive rounds turn up nothing new — catches long tails that a fixed-N loop misses
- **Judge panels:** generate several independent solution attempts from different angles, score them with parallel judges, and synthesize from the winner while grafting good ideas from runners-up
- **Multi-modal sweep:** run several differently-angled searches in parallel (by container, by content, by entity, by time) since no single search strategy finds everything

---

## Use Cases

Anthropic and early adopters cite: codebase-wide bug hunts, large-scale migrations, profiler-guided optimization audits, security audits, and cross-checked research reports. One widely cited (if extreme) example: a workflow-driven agent architecture rewriting roughly 750,000 lines of code over six days by decomposing the migration into per-file pipelines with independent verification stages.

---

## Availability

Dynamic workflows require **Claude Code v2.1.154 or later**, and are available on all paid plans — via Anthropic's API directly, or through Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry.

---

## Why It Matters

This playground's own wiki-maintenance automation is a cautionary counterexample: it runs as a single linear agent turn rather than a workflow, and — per the July 7, 2026 lint pass on this wiki — has been branching fresh from a stale base every day for over a month without ever merging, so each run's additions have been silently discarded. A pipeline-based workflow (fetch state -> research -> write -> verify-no-duplicate -> commit) with an explicit merge/PR stage would have caught that structural failure far earlier, since the control flow — not a fresh agent's ad hoc judgment — would own the process end to end.
